Beállítom Szergej Lavrov orosz külügyminiszter vasárnap azt mondta, hogy a Nyugat által Moszkva ellen felhozott vádak, miszerint az ország részt vett a németországi lipcsei repülőtéren történt drónincidensben, „nagyjából egy valódi háború kezdetét jelentik” – írja a Reuters a TASS állami hírügynökségre hivatkozva. „Merz összes nyilatkozata arról, hogy Németországot ismét Európa vezető katonai hatalmává kell tenni – ezeket most gyakorlatba is ültetik. Ő tulajdonképpen hadat üzen nekünk” – mondta Lavrov, utalva Friedrich Merz német kancellárra. A német kormány szeptember 1-jén közölte, hogy megállapította : Oroszország felelős a múlt hónapban a lipcsei repülőtéren történt drónos támadási kísérletért. Oroszország alaptalannak minősítette a német vádakat, és azzal vádolta Berlint, bizonyítékokat hamisított, hogy Oroszországot felelőssé tegye a támadásért. Németország a történteket nem hagyta szó nélkül, több diplomáciai választ is adtak: bezáratják a bonni orosz főkonzulátust és a Berlinben működő Orosz Ház kulturális központot, emellett pedig megszigorítják az orosz állampolgárok beutazására vonatkozó ellenőrzéseket. Johann Wadephul azt is bejelentette, hogy bekérették Oroszország berlini nagykövetét. Újabb közös európai szankciós lépésekről is tárgyaltak. A németek diplomáciai szinten reagáltak, de a Telexnek nyilatkozó szakértő szerint ennél többet is tesznek. „Az orosz reakció pedig most az, hogy akkor ők ebbe beleállnak, és jelzik a németeknek, hogy hajlandók tovább eszkalálni a helyzetet” – mondta szeptember elején Jójárt Krisztián biztonságpolitikai szakértő, a Svéd Nemzetvédelmi Egyetem kutatója. Szerinte Oroszország ezzel éppen azt teszteli, hogy meddig hajlandók elmenni a németek. A lipcsei repülőtéren még augusztus elején történt támadáskísérlet: közepes méretű drón repült be a repülőtér területére, amin robbanószert is találtak . Az eszköz éppen az ukránok Antonov teherszállító gépe mellé zuhant le, miután a gép szárnyának csapódott, de nem robbant fel. Az erről készült képek, videók bejárták a világsajtót . A lipcsei reptér egyébként stratégiai jelentőségű, mert rengeteg fegyverszállítmányt innen visznek Ukrajnába. A drón ott ért földet, ahol a legnagyobbat robbanhat egy megtankolt repülő, így már akkor biztos volt, hogy bárki állt is a háttérben, kemény üzenetet akart küldeni . Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief STOCKHOLM, SWEDEN ( Worthy News ) – Sweden’s parliament has approved a constitutional right to abortion, despite longstanding opposition to the practice from the Catholic Church and other Christians. The Riksdag, Sweden’s 349-member legislature, voted 292 to 51 to amend the country’s constitution, making abortion a fundamental right and freedom from January 1, 2027, Worthy News learned. Wednesday’s vote places the Nordic nation among a small number of European countries explicitly protecting abortion in their constitutions, after France became the first country in the world to do so in March 2024. Swedish lawmakers approved the measure as part of a broader constitutional package that also permits future legislation to revoke citizenship in certain circumstances and restrict groups involved in serious crime. In a statement obtained by Worthy News, the Riksdag confirmed that “the right to abortion will be introduced into the Instrument of Government as a new fundamental right and freedom.” SWEDEN’S ABORTION LAW The legislature added that the constitutional amendments “will come into force on 1 January 2027.” Abortion protections will become part of Sweden’s Instrument of Government, one of the fundamental laws forming the country’s constitution. Under existing Swedish legislation, pregnant women can obtain abortions on request through the 18th week of pregnancy. After that point, permission from the National Board of Health and Welfare is required, and abortions are generally prohibited once the fetus is considered capable of surviving outside the womb. The constitutional amendment does not itself change those limits but establishes abortion as a protected right, with its exercise governed by legislation. Sweden’s decision follows France’s March 2024 constitutional amendment guaranteeing the freedom to have an abortion. FRANCE SETS PRECEDENT French lawmakers approved the measure amid international debate over abortion restrictions, particularly following the United States Supreme Court’s 2022 decision overturning the nationwide constitutional protection previously established under Roe v. Wade. Elsewhere in Europe, abortion remains governed by differing constitutional provisions and national laws, reflecting disagreements over the protection of unborn life. Hungary, for example, takes a different constitutional approach. Article II of its Fundamental Law states that “the life of the foetus shall be protected from the moment of conception.” Yet abortion remains legal in Hungary under specified conditions, generally during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, with later procedures permitted in certain circumstances. On Thursday, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced plans to amend a 2022 rule requiring women seeking abortions to receive confirmation from a healthcare provider of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly interpreted as a fetal heartbeat. HUNGARY’S ABORTION DEBATE Magyar said the requirement had failed to reduce abortions and had caused additional trauma. However, Christian and pro-life organisations in Hungary criticised Magyar’s proposed changes. Imre Téglásy, founder of the Alpha Alliance, defended the existing fetal heartbeat requirement, arguing that women should be fully informed before undergoing an abortion. In August, the Hungarian Catholic Bishops’ Conference reaffirmed its opposition to abortion, declaring that human life must be protected from conception until natural death. The bishops also urged the government to provide practical assistance to pregnant women and families facing difficult circumstances. France’s constitutional amendment also drew opposition from the Catholic Church, which teaches that human life must be respected and protected from conception. VATICAN OPPOSES ABORTION Following the French vote, the Vatican’s Pontifical Academy for Life supported the French bishops’ opposition and called for greater assistance to women facing difficult pregnancies. The academy stressed that protecting human life should remain a central responsibility of governments and society. Catholic teaching has consistently opposed direct abortion, maintaining that unborn human life possesses inherent dignity and must be protected. Its position contrasts with arguments advanced by abortion-rights advocates, who maintain that access to abortion is essential to women’s bodily autonomy, healthcare and reproductive freedom. In April 2024, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for the right to abortion to be included in the European Union’s Charter of Fundamental Rights. EU ABORTION RIGHTS DEBATE However, such a change would require unanimous agreement among EU member states, whose national abortion laws and constitutional approaches differ considerably. Beyond abortion, Sweden’s constitutional package authorises future laws allowing citizenship to be revoked from dual nationals who obtained Swedish citizenship through false or misleading information or were convicted of crimes seriously harming Sweden’s vital interests. Another amendment permits restrictions on freedom of association involving organisations engaged in serious crime. Under Sweden’s constitution, amendments must be approved twice by parliament, with a national election held between the two votes. Lawmakers gave their first approval on May 20, 2026. Following September’s general election, the newly elected parliament approved the amendments again on Wednesday, completing the constitutional process. Members of the Left Party and Green Party opposed the combined amendments, arguing particularly that the proposed citizenship provisions went too far and risked weakening protections for citizens, despite supporting constitutional abortion protections. Sweden’s decision marks a significant shift in its constitutional treatment of abortion, highlighting contrasting approaches to the issue across Europe.
